newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr edges lower in Tokyo, but retains bullish mood.
newsitem.headline: Dlr edges lower in Tokyo, but retains bullish mood.

text.p: 0319 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0300 GMT
The dollar drifted down by midday on Wednesday in Tokyo, but its underlying trend stayed strong against the yen, dealers said.

The dollar/mark rate was weighed down as long holders of the greenback unwound some positions ahead of a statement later today by the German cabinet which is expected to endorse a strong mark and a strong euro.
In New York on Tuesday, the dollar fell when Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler told reporters in Germany that the dollar's rally may have become excessive.
Zeitler added that Germany wants a strong mark and German Finance Minister Theo Waigel later told Reuters the German cabinet will make such a statement on the mark and euro.

The dollar should be supported as firm bids were expected to emerge around 1.7840/50 marks, slightly above the level where stop-loss selling was placed at 1.7830 marks, dealers said. The dollar closed at 1.7930/40 marks and 115.74/79 yen in New York on Tuesday.

The dollar/yen rate was trapped in a boxed range, with sales by exporters and hedge-related sales by investors capping the upper side, while it was well-protected by bargain-hunters and purchases by Japanese trust banks on dips, dealers said.
Tokyo operators, who had lagged behind in building long positions following rapid and unexpected rises overnight, were buying dollars repeatedly on falls against the yen.

"Interbank operators, including trust banks, are cautiously buying now. They are cautious of buying aggressively ahead of the release of Japanese and U.S. trade figures (on Thursday and Friday respectively)," a Japanese city bank dealer said.
"The dollar's rise to 116 yen overnight was unexpected as many Tokyo operators have bet the dollar will edge downward ahead of the trade figures," the dealer said.

Dealers said the impact of U.S.-Japan trade issues may be limited after a series of recent comments from newly appointed Vice Finance Minister for International Affairs Eisuke Sakakibara, who has repeatedly said ministry has no intention of using foreign exchange rates as a trade tool.
But dealers said operators in Tokyo were not fully confident about boosting their dollar-long positions aggressively due to concerns over Japan's ballooning surplus.
